claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by formation of a dense passive film enriched in oxide-forming elements.
Niobium enrichment increases passive-film compactness in TiHfZrNb alloys.
A Nb-enriched passive film reduces point-defect density and defect mobility, thereby improving resistance to dissolution and pitting.
Chromium enrichment produces an analogous compact, protective passive film.
The passive film provides a hard, adherent surface that directly resists abrasive wear.
Increasing Nb or Cr content is the proposed compositional intervention for improving simultaneous wear-corrosion resistance.
The continuity and Nb/Cr-oxide enrichment of the passive film mediates both mechanical wear response and electrochemical response.
Enhanced niobium promotes rapid initial passivation and greater surface coverage.
Enhanced Nb/Cr improves repassivation during mechanical wear.
Increasing Nb content can improve both tribological behavior and electrochemical stability.
Increasing Cr content will lower corrosion current density relative to a lower-Cr baseline.
Increasing Nb or Cr will reduce wear volume during simultaneous wear-corrosion testing.
Lower-Nb alloys form a less compact and less protective passive film than matched higher-Nb alloys.
Lower Nb/Cr concentrations cause both higher corrosion rates and greater wear-related material loss.
The protective mechanism should operate in environments that permit passive-film formation, including neutral to mildly acidic solutions.
The mechanism may fail when an extremely aggressive environment disrupts the passive film faster than it can repassivate.
The mechanism may fail in alloys with unstable microstructures.
Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in both corrosion current density and wear volume, or failure to observe improved passive-film characteristics, would falsify the hypothesis.
